summary.title: The Five Lies Analysis
summary.one_liner: Learn why the Five Whys root cause technique gives inconsistent results when applied blindly or fixed into a postmortem template, and what to use instead (debriefing prompts that build a story of the incident).
keywords: field guide to understanding human error
takeaways: Five Whys answers differ widely depending on who runs it, so the results are not repeatable.
The fixed number five can limit investigation depth; keep digging when it adds understanding.
Putting Five Whys into a template solidifies its limits and carries its downsides into postmortems.
Root causes are rarely singular; aim for an inside-out understanding of the incident and broad action items.
Debriefing facilitation prompts (Dekker, cited by Allspaw) can structure learning from multiple system angles.
summary.summary: The article uses a fictional Acme News outage to show how five different engineers (SRE, backend, frontend/product, cloud infrastructure, core libraries) each run a Five Whys analysis and reach different root causes and action items. The author argues this shows the technique is not repeatable, that the number five arbitrarily limits depth, and that embedding it in a postmortem template restricts investigations. Instead, the author suggests building a detailed story of the incident using debriefing facilitation prompts from Sidney Dekker's Field Guide to Understanding Human Error, as recommended by John Allspaw in The Infinite Hows. The piece is an essay with a narrative example rather than a hands-on tutorial.
